WALKTHROUGH.title: Pacsana — a guided tour
WALKTHROUGH.subtitle: How the app reads a person’s daily movement, and how family and carers stay in the picture without standing over them.
WALKTHROUGH.disclaimer: Sample walkthrough for demonstration. The screens are mock-ups drawn for this demo, not the real product, and all names, times and figures are invented.

STEPS.title: The daily picture
STEPS.alt: App home screen showing steps, sleep and a trip out of the house
STEPS.lifeAlt: An older woman standing in her kitchen on an ordinary morning
STEPS.voice: Here is a quick tour of the Pacsana mobile app, and how it reads your daily movement.
body: A small worn sensor picks up ordinary movement around the house — getting up, moving between rooms, sitting down, going out.
The app turns that into one plain-language summary: how you slept, how much you have moved, whether you have been out.
No cameras, no microphones, nothing to remember to switch on.
STEPS.note: One screen answers the question everybody actually asks: is today a normal day?

STEPS.title: Your circle
STEPS.alt: A list of people who can see the information, with their access levels
STEPS.lifeAlt: The same woman at home with her daughter and a care worker, both holding phones
STEPS.voice: See how easy it is to stay connected, so family and carers know you are well.
body: You choose who is in your circle and how much each person sees — everything, or only urgent alerts.
Family members and care workers use the same app, so nobody is relying on a phone call being answered.
Access can be changed or switched off at any time.

STEPS.title: Rest and movement
STEPS.alt: Two bar charts: sleep hours and active hours across the week
STEPS.lifeAlt: A split scene: walking outdoors by day, asleep in bed by night
STEPS.voice: Are you resting well at night, and are you mobile during the day?
body: Night and day are shown together, because one explains the other.
A week at a glance makes a pattern obvious in a way a single night never does.
The app compares you with your own normal, not with an average stranger.

STEPS.title: Sleep in detail
STEPS.alt: Sleep detail screen with time asleep, settled percentage and restless periods
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman asleep in bed with a bedside lamp on low
body: Time asleep, how settled the night was, and how often it was interrupted.
A run of restless nights is usually the first sign that something else is going on.
Carers see the same view, so a conversation starts from the same facts.

STEPS.title: Skin health
STEPS.alt: Screen showing time spent in one position and prompts to move
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman seated in an armchair, with a clock showing time passing
body: Long spells in the same position are the main risk factor for pressure damage.
The app tracks the longest unbroken spell and how often position changes through the day.
A gentle prompt is easier to act on than a district nurse visit three weeks later.

STEPS.title: Night-time trips
STEPS.alt: Screen showing bathroom trips last night and across the week
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman walking to the bathroom at night, lit by a bedside lamp
STEPS.voice: How often did you visit the bathroom last night?
body: Trips to the bathroom at night are counted and timed.
A sudden change can point to an infection, a medication effect or a fall risk in the dark.
Shown as a trend, so one unusual night does not cause alarm.

STEPS.title: Getting outside
STEPS.alt: Screen showing a trip out of the house and outdoor time for the week
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman walking outdoors with a stick, past a tree
STEPS.voice: Are you getting outside to exercise?
body: Trips beyond the front door are recorded separately from moving around indoors.
Time outdoors, number of trips, and how that compares with last week.
Getting out matters for strength, mood and appetite, so it is worth counting on its own.

STEPS.title: Company
STEPS.alt: Screen showing hours spent with other people and recent visits
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman and her daughter having tea at the table
body: Time with other people — visitors at home, and time spent out.
Isolation creeps up slowly, which is exactly the kind of change a weekly trend catches.
It also shows the family something useful: the weekends are quiet.

STEPS.title: What might help
STEPS.alt: Screen showing three suggestions, each with the reason behind it
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman walking outdoors with her daughter after lunch
STEPS.voice: The app also gives advice on what might help improve your health.
body: Suggestions come from your own data, and each one says why it is being offered.
Small, specific and doable — a short walk after lunch, standing up every hour.
Advice you can ignore, which is rather the point: it is guidance, not instruction.
STEPS.note: Suggestions are general wellbeing prompts, not medical advice.

STEPS.title: Reports
STEPS.alt: Report screen splitting activity inside and outside the home against the WHO target
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman rising from her chair indoors and walking outdoors
STEPS.voice: A set of reports looks at exercise both inside and outside the home, and checks whether you are meeting the WHO goals.
body: Activity is split between inside and outside the home, because they mean different things.
Progress is measured against the World Health Organization’s weekly activity guideline.
The report can be shared with a GP or physio, which saves a lot of guessing at an appointment.

STEPS.title: Mobility
STEPS.alt: Screen showing daily steps, walking pace and a fall-risk estimate
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman stumbling and catching herself against the worktop
STEPS.voice: Are you moving enough? How fast are you getting around? And how likely are you to fall?
body: Three measures that matter as people get older: how much, how fast, and how steadily.
Walking pace is one of the better early indicators of declining health, and it changes slowly enough to spot.
Fall risk is an estimate built from pace, steadiness and night-time activity.

STEPS.title: Watching around the clock
STEPS.alt: Screen showing a 24-hour activity ribbon and what the pattern indicates
STEPS.lifeAlt: Day and night together: walking above, asleep below, a clock between
STEPS.voice: Carers cannot be there all the time, but Pacsana analyses the data 24/7.
body: The analysis runs continuously, including the hours when nobody is in the house.
It compares today against the person’s own established pattern rather than a generic threshold.
Family and carers see the same picture, updated as the day goes on.

STEPS.title: Alerts as they happen
STEPS.alt: Alerts screen showing an urgent alert and two informational ones
STEPS.lifeAlt: The daughter receiving an alert on her phone while her mother sits at home
STEPS.voice: And they can be notified of specific events that happen in real time.
body: Specific events trigger a notification: no movement when there should be, leaving the house late, returning home.
Each person in the circle chooses which alerts they receive, so nobody is woken for a normal night.
Every alert says what happened, when, and what is unusual about it.

STEPS.title: Peace of mind
STEPS.alt: Closing screen showing an all-clear for the day
STEPS.lifeAlt: The woman and her daughter together at home
STEPS.voice: Pacsana gives peace of mind, acting as their eyes and ears when family or carers cannot be there.
body: Most days, the answer is simply that everything is fine — and knowing that is the point.
The person keeps their independence and their privacy. The family stops guessing.
When something does change, everybody hears about it early enough to do something.
STEPS.note: Eyes and ears when you cannot be there.
